name: Saga Dawa at Kailash
when: Full moon of the 4th Tibetan month, usually late May or June
summary: Saga Dawa marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing. At Kailash, thousands of pilgrims gather at Tarboche on the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month to watch the great prayer-flag pole lowered, re-dressed and raised, then begin the parikrama together.
body: Saga Dawa is the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist year, and its full moon, Saga Dawa Düchen, is when merit from good actions is believed to multiply many times over. Across Tibet, people give alms, free animals, recite mantras and walk koras. At Mount Kailash the day is focused on Tarboche, the tall flagpole at the start of the parikrama near Yam Dwar, a few kilometres west of Darchen.

On the morning of the festival, monks and local men lower the pole, strip off last year's flags and wrap it in new ones, while crowds of Tibetan pilgrims, nomads in their best clothes and visitors from India and Nepal watch from the plain. When the pole is raised, using ropes and sometimes vehicles, people throw lungta paper prayers into the air and cheer. Tibetans believe a perfectly upright pole means a good year; a lean is read as a warning.

Many pilgrims begin their parikrama straight after the ceremony, so the trail on Saga Dawa is busier than on any other day, and accommodation at Darchen, Dirapuk and Zuthulpuk fills fast. Permits for Kailash around the festival are in high demand and sometimes restricted. The date follows the lunar calendar and moves each year; check current status before you travel.
tips: Book at least four months ahead; Darchen and parikrama guesthouses sell out around Saga Dawa.
Arrive at Tarboche early in the morning with warm clothes, water and snacks; the ceremony can run for hours.
Expect a crowded trail on Dolma La on the festival day and the day after; walk steadily and keep your group together.

faqs.q: When is Saga Dawa at Kailash?
faqs.a: Saga Dawa falls on the full moon of the fourth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in late May or June. The exact date changes every year. Our Saga Dawa yatra is timed so the group reaches Darchen the day before. Check current status before you travel, as permits around the festival can be restricted.

faqs.q: What happens at Tarboche on Saga Dawa?
faqs.a: The great prayer-flag pole at Tarboche is lowered, its old flags removed and new ones tied on, then it is raised again before crowds of pilgrims. Tibetans watch whether it stands straight as an omen for the year. Lungta prayers are thrown and many pilgrims start the parikrama right after.

faqs.q: Is Kailash parikrama harder during Saga Dawa?
faqs.a: The route is the same, but crowds make the trail slower, especially on the climb to Dolma La, and guesthouses are full. Ponies and porters are in high demand. Start early each day and book everything through your agency well in advance.

faqs.q: Is Saga Dawa a Hindu or Buddhist festival?
faqs.a: Saga Dawa is a Tibetan Buddhist festival commemorating the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and parinirvana. Hindu pilgrims at Kailash join the occasion as an especially auspicious time for parikrama and darshan, and the shared reverence for the mountain makes it a gathering of many faiths.

name: Shoton (Yoghurt) Festival
when: Late 6th to early 7th Tibetan month, usually August
summary: Shoton, the yoghurt festival, opens at dawn with the unveiling of a giant thangka on the hillside at Drepung Monastery, followed by days of Tibetan opera and picnics in Lhasa's Norbulingka. It usually falls in August and is one of the busiest weeks in Lhasa.
body: Shoton began centuries ago as a feast at which lay people offered yoghurt to monks emerging from their summer retreat. Over time it grew to include Tibetan opera, or Ache Lhamo, and today it is Lhasa's best-known festival. It runs for about a week from the end of the sixth Tibetan month, which usually means August in the Western calendar, sometimes early September.

On the first morning, crowds climb the hill behind Drepung Monastery in the dark. As the sun rises, monks carry out and unroll an enormous thangka of the Buddha across a framework on the slope, revealing it for a few hours while pilgrims throw khata scarves and offer prayers. Juniper smoke drifts over the crowd, and families share yoghurt and tea. It is a striking sight but a crowded one, with steep paths and tight security.

For the following days, opera troupes perform in the Norbulingka park, the Dalai Lamas' former summer palace, and families picnic under tents in the gardens. Hotels and Potala tickets are in high demand during the festival week, and dates are published only a few months ahead. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Start the climb to Drepung around 4–5 am with a headtorch; the thangka unveiling happens at sunrise.
Book hotels and Potala tickets as early as possible for festival week; prices rise sharply.
Carry your passport for security checks and keep valuables close in the dense crowd.

faqs.q: When is the Shoton Festival in Lhasa?
faqs.a: Shoton begins on the 30th day of the sixth Tibetan month and lasts about a week, which usually falls in August and occasionally early September. Exact dates are published a few months ahead. Check current status before you travel and book Lhasa hotels early for that week.

faqs.q: Where is the thangka unveiled during Shoton?
faqs.a: The giant thangka is unveiled at dawn on the hillside behind Drepung Monastery, about 8 km west of central Lhasa. Crowds climb up in the dark to see it as the sun rises. The thangka is displayed for a few hours and then rolled up again.

faqs.q: Why is it called the yoghurt festival?
faqs.a: Sho means yoghurt and ton means feast or banquet. The festival began as an occasion for lay people to offer yoghurt to monks at the end of their summer retreat. Families still eat yoghurt during the festival, alongside picnics and Tibetan opera in the Norbulingka.

Yes, foreigners on a permitted Tibet tour with a licensed guide can attend the thangka unveiling and the opera at Norbulingka. Expect very large crowds and security checks. Tibet tour permits are in high demand during the festival, so apply early through your agency.
